Thank you, Madam Co-Chair. Excellencies, in wartime and peacetime alike, the use and testing of nuclear weapons have resulted in catastrophic and enduring harm to individuals, communities, and the environment, with consequences extending across borders and generations. Impacts encompass both radiological and non-radiological consequences, including intergenerational and psychosocial impacts, as well as cultural and displacement-related harm affecting communities far removed from the use or testing of nuclear weapons in both place and time. All victims of human rights violations, including from nuclear impacts, have the right to access to effective remedy for violation of their human rights in line with the basic principles and guidelines on the right to remedy and reparation, for victims of gross violation of international human rights law and serious violation of international humanitarian law adopted by the General Assembly in 2005. Our office has seen firsthand the importance of a human rights-based approach to addressing the immediate and intergenerational impacts of nuclear weapons through four years of implementing a Human Rights Council mandate on the nuclear legacy in the Marshall Islands. 67 known nuclear tests were conducted in the Marshall Islands between 1946 and 1958. Together, they had a total yield of approximately 7,232 times the explosive power of the atomic bomb dropped on Hiroshima. The consequences have been lasting and profound, affecting the enjoyment of the rights to health, life, health, housing, food, and the right to clean, healthy, and sustainable environments. When the environment is degraded, the impact does not end with the soil or the sea. It affects where people may safely live, what they can eat, whether they can return home, and whether traditional ways of life can continue. Environmental remediation, therefore, is essential for restoring the conditions necessary for the full enjoyment and realization of human rights. In our work with the Marshall Islands and its National Nuclear Commission, and consultations with affected communities in the Marshall Islands and beyond, we have seen the importance of a transitional justice approach. Justice for nuclear harm does not come in singular form. but through the interrelated elements of truth, accountability, reparations, and guarantees of non-repetition. Victim assistance and environmental remediations must be understood to embrace all these elements. Truth-telling and memorialization, as well as of countries owning up to past actions, are critical parts of a transitional justice approach. Victim assistance cannot be separated from participation. In our consultations, Marshallese have used storytelling, poetry, and art to articulate what nuclear justice means to them. Such lived experience of communities highlights the importance of indigenous justice systems and cultural practices in addressing nuclear impacts, especially for groups in vulnerable situations. Distinguished delegates, radiological harm does not affect every person equally. In the Marshall Islands, OISHR has heard testimonies of miscarriages, stillbirth, and of children born with congenital conditions. Women and girls whose health and traditional roles have been disproportionately affected by nuclear impacts must have meaningful roles in shaping the responses intended to serve them. Victims must be engaged not only to identify nuclear harms, but as agents of change. This work also requires cooperation across jurisdictions. Nuclear fallout does not respect national borders, and affected communities today extend well beyond the places where nuclear weapons were used or tested. Excellencies, as nuclear impacts extend across borders and generation, so too must our cooperation. Victim assistance and environmental remediations are neither acts of benevolence or mere aspiration. They are human rights obligations to current and future generations. Thank you.

I thank the distinguished representative of OHCHR. We will now proceed to hear statements from representatives of affected communities and civil societies. I now give the floor to Miss Mary Dixon, affected community member and down winter from Utah.

Yes. It's an honor to be here today. Thank you. As she said, I'm an American downwinder, a survivor of radioactive fallout from 928 nuclear weapons detonated on our own soil for over four decades at the Nevada Test Site, just 60 miles from Las Vegas. I grew up in Salt Lake City, Utah, during the years of above-ground testing. We ate vegetables from the garden, drank fresh milk from a local dairy, splashed in rainwater, and mixed sugar with snow to pretend it was ice cream. How were we to know that radioactive fallout was coming down with that rain and snow, contaminating our food and embedding itself into our bodies? We trusted our government when it told us there was no danger. In my late 20s, I was diagnosed with thyroid cancer. Surgeons cut out my thyroid and surrounding lymph nodes. To destroy any remaining cancer cells, they gave me radioactive iodine to drink. On my hospital door and wristband was the radiation symbol. I was the radioactive material. During a body scan, I watched my ovaries light up. I never could have children. Years later, new tumors led to a complete hysterectomy. I've been sliced, radiated, and scooped out. I've buried and mourned the dead, comforted and advocated for the living, and worried with each ache, pain, and lump that I am getting sick again. But I'm one of the lucky ones. I survived. My older sister, like so many others, did not. Before she died at 46, we counted 54 people in our childhood neighborhood plagued with cancers and other serious illnesses as well as infertility, children with leukemia and birth defects. My younger sister is now battling a rare cancer that has spread throughout her body. Sadly, our stories are far too common. As survivors, it is urgent that we keep them alive. When we talk about victims and assistance, compensation matters. It's not simply about money, because no amount can give us back our health, the loved ones we've buried, nor can it ease the sorrow we carry. Compensation says we acknowledge what happened to you. We believe you. You never should have been harmed. It also carries something victims have waited far too long to hear: an apology. Medical support also must be part of meaningful victim assistance. The illnesses didn't end when the testing stopped. People exposed decades ago are still being diagnosed. Cancers return, they spread, health complications arise. We live with a constant fear of what the next medical scan or test may reveal. Then we are saddled with crippling medical bills. We should not have to struggle to pay for health care that the actions of governments made necessary. We should also learn from the failures of existing compensation programs. In 1990, the U.S. finally provided partial compensation to some downwinders, but only within narrowly defined geographic boundaries and only for certain cancers. People often ask me, how do I know I'm a downwinder? I tell them, because the U.S. government says you are. Government maps showed how far the jet streams carried the fallout. They knew it spread across the country far beyond the boundaries they drew. After pushing for years, we recently saw compensation expanded, but countless communities are still excluded by arbitrary lines on a map or because their disease isn't the right one. And we know radiation did not stop at county, state, or national borders. We know it didn't respect political boundaries, and justice cannot be confined by them either. For years, I've listened to the stories of nuclear survivors from across the U.S. and around the world. I hear the same heartbreaking themes: disease, too many dead, secrecy, denial, and the burden of proof placed on the victims. Victim assistance can begin to lift that burden. It can acknowledge what happened, compensate those harmed, and provide lifelong health care and screenings. And it can remediate the contaminated lands where people live, grow food, and raise their children. These are not acts of charity. They are obligations of justice. We can't undo what was done to us at the hands of nuclear nations. But nations can decide whether we, the victims, continue to carry these burdens alone. They can also decide whether communities worldwide will again be deemed expendable, causing new generations to suffer the same tragedies we have endured. To me, the ultimate justice is to at last bring the age of nuclear weapons to an end. If I've learned anything from being a survivor, it's this, we all live downwind. Thank you.

Under Secretary General for Disarmament Affairs, Excellencies, distinguished delegates, ladies and gentlemen, my name is Ooma Johnson, a proud granddaughter and great-granddaughter of nuclear survivors from Kiritimati Island. I stand before you not as a youth from Kiribati advocating for a world free of nuclear weapons, but also as someone whose family history has been touched by the nuclear legacy of the Pacific. For families like mine and many other affected communities across the world, including those in the Marshall Islands, Kazakhstan, Japan, and elsewhere, Nuclear testing is not simply something that happened in the past. Its legacy continues through our stories, concerns for our health and environment, and the well-being of generations that come after us. Today, I would like to draw our attention to one important thing. Behind every policy, every treaty, and every discussion about nuclear weapons, there are people, families, communities, and generations living with the consequences of decisions they did not make. One clear lesson we have learned is that victim assistance cannot be temporary. Affected communities need access to proper health care, regular medical screening, psychological and emotional support, and social and economic assistance. We must also better understand the long-term and intergenerational impacts of nuclear weapons. As a fourth-generation nuclear survivor, this issue is both deeply personal and important to me. Those who came before us experienced the nuclear age firsthand, but younger generations today continue to live with its legacy and are still searching for answers about what it means for our health and the generations that will follow. We therefore strongly encourage greater investment in independent scientific and medical research and long-term health monitoring. But this work must also be transparent and inclusive. Nuclear survivors and affected communities should not simply be sources of stories, information or data for others to benefit from. They should know how their information is being used, have access to the findings and be included in decisions about how their stories and data are collected, preserved or shared. Research should ultimately benefit the communities who make it possible. But health is only one part of this issue. Our environment matters too. For us as Pacific people, our connection to the land and ocean is deeply rooted in who we are. Our ocean feeds us. Our land connects us to our families and ancestors. They carry our traditions, livelihood, and identity. When these environments are damaged or contaminated, we risk losing part of who we are. Environmental remediation must therefore go hand in hand with victim assistance. We encourage continued monitoring of affected land, water, marine resources, and food sources with findings shared transparently with affected communities. Excellencies and distinguished delegates, Article six and seven of the treaty on the prohibition of nuclear weapons provide an important pathway for victim assistance, environmental remediation, and international cooperation. Affected states have an important role in supporting their communities through health services, environmental monitoring, and the preservation of information, but especially for small island developing states with limited resources, this work cannot be carried alone. We therefore call for stronger international solidarity and cooperation, including financial and technical assistance, health services, scientific expertise, capacity building, environmental monitoring, and knowledge sharing. We also call upon states that used or tested nuclear weapons to take greater responsibility in addressing the consequences that remain, through access to historical records and scientific data, independent research, stronger health services, and sustained support for environmental remediation. We welcome continued work towards an international trust fund for victim assistance and environmental remediation as an important step towards international commitments, towards turning international commitments into practical support. It means listening to them when priorities are decided, including them in research and allowing them to participate in the design of assistance and remediation programs. It means recognizing affected communities not only as victims, but as partners in finding solutions. excellencies and distinguished delegates. Distinguished delegates, Peace Boat welcomes the first United Nations meeting on nuclear victim assistance and environmental remediation. As a Japan-based international civil society organization, Peace Boat has traveled the world since 2008 with over 170 hibakusha and other global nuclear survivors. When considering international support, understanding Japan's relief system for hibakusha is crucial. While providing meaningful medical support, its significant limitations offer valuable lessons. First is the recognition that Japan provides relief for hibakusha, not state compensation. Nihon Hidankyo has continuously called for state compensation, acknowledging government war responsibility, which remains unrealized. Second is the issue of official recognition. Survivors certified by the government are issued an atomic bomb survivor certificate, and in principle are eligible for free medical care. However, people beyond specific geographic bounds from the hypocenter were excluded, sparking longstanding litigation by residents. In 2021, a political decision in Hiroshima recognized black rain victims. However, this issue remains unresolved in Nagasaki. Disputes over the scope of certification are closely connected to evaluating internal radiation exposure, which must also be considered in victim certification decisions. Third is the certification of atomic bomb disease for survivors who develop specific illnesses like cancer or leukemia. The Japanese government grants certain allowances to the individuals in such cases. However, hibakusha organizations have long disputed this system, arguing that the scope is too narrow and the criteria too strict. Fourth is relief for non-Japanese and overseas hibakusha. Japan's colonial rule until 1945 brought many non-Japanese people, including from the Korean peninsula, to Hiroshima and Nagasaki, where they consequently experienced the atomic bombings. Post-war, they ceased to have Japanese citizenship and were excluded from relief. Hibakusha, among the many Japanese immigrants to the Pacific and the Americas, also received either no or only limited relief. Through repeated lawsuits, these groups eventually gained legal recognition equivalent to hibakusha in Japan. The starting point for all victim assistance is defining who is recognized. Japan's experience shows that while official definitions may be narrow, victims themselves, as well as civil society in affected areas, advocate for broader rights. Civil society and diverse impacted voices must therefore be involved in the design of victim assistance policies. Furthermore, nuclear harm extends beyond the effects of radiation itself. Hibakusha are also victims of war, suffering blast and heat injuries alongside destroyed infrastructure, families, and communities, resulting in long-term social, economic, psychological, and intergenerational impacts. In this context, a gender perspective is also vital. Women and girls are not only particularly vulnerable to the effects of radiation, but have also experienced caregiving burdens, psychological impacts, and gender-based violence. These points reaffirm that victims and affected communities must continuously participate in the design and implementation of all nuclear victim assistance systems. The voices of those with lived experiences, as well as those who find it difficult to speak out, must be listened to actively. We recommend that countries, including Japan, exchange information in order to verify, evaluate, and compare existing assistance systems and identify improvements. We call on countries that have used or tested nuclear weapons to share detailed information regarding these actions and for all data on damage and environmental contamination to be shared with victims, affected communities, and countries. And we call those welcoming discussions within the framework of the TPNW towards the establishment of an international trust fund for victims' assistance. Thank you very much.

Thank. Thank you very much for the opportunity to contribute to this important discussion. Today's meeting represents an important moment to reflect on and advance nuclear justice. When we speak about the legacy of nuclear weapons use and testing, we have extensive evidence of the devastating consequences for human health, the environment, communities, and future generation. These impacts on human health are not merely physical, but also psychological and social. The humanitarian consequences of the use and testing of nuclear weapons should never be a matter of controversy. Today, we would like to use this opportunity to highlight two essential dimensions of nuclear justice. First, creating meaningful spaces for listening to affected communities. Second, strengthening education. For Sokagaka International, recognizing the dignity, knowledge, and agency of those who have experienced the consequences of nuclear weapons firsthand is a crucial step for nuclear justice. Affected communities cannot be seen only as recipients of assistance or subjects of research. They are knowledge holders. Their experiences tell us not only what happened, but what nuclear harm means in people's lives. The loss of homes and livelihoods, the disruption of communities and cultures, the impacts on health and well-being, and the fears and uncertainties passed from one generation to the next. For this reason, creating meaningful spaces for affected communities to be part of decision-making processes, speak, share their perspective and knowledge of their community's needs, and for others to genuinely listen and learn is itself an important dimension of justice. For decades, SGI has collected and shared the testimonies of hibakusha through publications, videos, exhibition, and dialogue. We have also organized opportunities for young people to listen directly to survivors and engage with their experiences. These encounters are not simply acts of remembrance. They create opportunities for younger generations to understand the humanitarian consequences of nuclear weapons, develop empathy, reflect on their own responsibilities, and inherit the determination of survivors that no one else should ever have to experience such suffering. Education about nuclear weapons must therefore go beyond the transmission of historical facts. It should include survivor-led storytelling, intergenerational dialogue, participatory learning, and spaces where young people can ask questions, listen, reflect, and take action. This is particularly urgent as many survivors are aging. Preserving their experiences is essential, but preservation alone is not enough. We must create opportunities for their knowledge and experiences to inform present and future decision making. At the same time, education should empower affected communities and young people to become active participants in shaping the policies that concern their lives and futures. Our experience working with young people has shown us that they are not simply looking for information. They are seeking meaningful opportunities to learn together, develop confidence and skills, and contribute to building peace. We therefore encourage governments, international organizations, and civil society to strengthen education and awareness raising on the humanitarian and environmental consequences of nuclear weapons, support initiative led by survivors and affected communities, create sustained spaces for dialogue among survivors, younger generations, policymakers, and wider society, and strengthen efforts toward nuclear disarmament by joining and supporting the TPNW and fulfilling obligation under Article 6 of the NPT. Nuclear justice requires that we do more than remember the harm of the past. We must listen to those who will experience it, learn from their experiences, and empower the next generation to ensure that such harm is never repeated. Thank you so much.
I thank the representative of Soka Gakkai International for his statement. I now give the floor to Mr. Seth Shelton, the International Campaign to Abolish Nuclear Weapons.

Distinguished delegates, we've gathered today to discuss the ongoing legacy of nuclear weapons and the needs to assist its survivors and remediate environments affected by nuclear weapons. We are gravely concerned about the catastrophic humanitarian and environmental consequences of nuclear weapons, which transcend national borders, pose grave implications for human survival and well-being, and are incompatible with the right to life. These consequences are more severe, cascading, long-lasting, geographically widespread, and complex than previously understood. involving long-term damage to the environment, socioeconomic and sustainable development, the global economy, food security, and the health of current and future generations. Survivors of nuclear weapons have suffered immensely and continue to suffer, including across generations. Nuclear weapons have a disproportionate impact on women and children, including as a result of ionizing radiation. ICAN underscores that detonating nuclear weapons for so-called testing must not be resumed for any reason or under any pretext, and we therefore urge all states to uphold the global norm against nuclear testing and to relegate its terrible legacy to history. Given that the catastrophic consequences of nuclear weapons cannot be adequately addressed, the only guarantee against the risks of these consequences is the total elimination of nuclear weapons. In this regard, we welcome the Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons as the only globally applicable treaty that unequivocally and categorically prohibits nuclear weapons, including their development, production, and detonation, and creates a framework for their total elimination. We also hail the landmark contribution of the TPNW as the first international treaty to recognize communities affected by nuclear weapons and to include victim assistance and environmental remediation from nuclear detonation harms as positive obligations of states parties under the TPNW's Article 6 and 7. We commend the work of TPNW states parties to operationalize these Articles 6 and 7, including through the informal working group established by the TPNW's Vienna Action Plan. As of today, the TPNW counts 100 countries as either states parties or signatories. We encourage all other countries to join the TPNW without delay and to contribute to the ongoing work of States Parties to advance victim assistance and environmental remediation. ICAN calls on all States, whether or not Parties to the TPNW, to participate in the first review conference of the TPNW from November 30th through December 4th of this year. where they may engage in a constructive dialogue with TPNW States Parties, advancing the only multilateral treaty that mandates assistance to communities affected by nuclear weapons. Furthermore, we assert that entry into force of the Comprehensive Nuclear Test Ban Treaty is essential and long overdue, and that it would complement the prohibition on nuclear weapons testing as contained in Article 1 of the TPNW. We call on all Annex II states under the CTBT to ratify it without additional delays or conditionalities, as further postponement is unacceptable, and we urge all states that have not signed or ratified the CTBT to do so without delay. We call on all states to collaborate through an inclusive approach with states, international organizations, indigenous peoples, people in non-self-governing territories, and civil society, including and especially people affected by nuclear detonations, in efforts to advance victim assistance and environmental remediation. In this regard, we encourage this meeting to adopt recommendations that respond to the specific proposals of representatives of affected communities including with respect to medical care, rehabilitation, psychological support, and social and economic inclusion. Thank you.
I thank the representative of ICAN for his statement. I now give the floor to Ms. Molly MacIntyre from the International Physicians for the Prevention of Nuclear War.

Distinguished Chair, Distinguished Chair, delegates and colleagues, since Trinity, the first nuclear detonation conducted 81 years ago today in the desert of the Tularosa Basin of present day New Mexico, nuclear weapons have had devastating and lasting impacts on human and planetary health. The entire nuclear weapons lifecycle has imposed severe long-term environmental costs and human suffering on innocent communities, spanning everything from the mining and milling of uranium and the storage of warheads to the constant threat of their use and their testing in the atmosphere, underwater, and underground. In the name of national security, more than 2,000 nuclear weapons were detonated near people's homes, hospitals, schools, places of worship, water supplies, fisheries, and farmland without the consent of downwind communities. Radioactive fallout knows no borders, poisons indiscriminately, and has fallen disproportionately on colonies, former colonies, and the territories of indigenous peoples and ethnic minorities. in the Marshall Islands, French Polynesia, and Kiribati, in Semipalatinsk, Kazakhstan, on traditional Western Shoshone land in Nevada, on Aboriginal lands in the Australian Outback, on Nenets land in the Russian Arctic, in the desert communities in Algeria, in the Uyghur land in China, and elsewhere. The health impacts of these detonations include elevated risks of cancer and leukemia, thyroid disease, birth defects, and reproductive complications, and other preventable harms, with women and children bearing disproportionate burden of their harm. Entire communities were displaced and not able to return to their homelands. Alarmingly, despite the widespread knowledge of these impacts and the decades-long moratorium on nuclear testing, some nuclear weapons states have signaled their intention to resume this deadly and destabilizing practice as part of today's renewed nuclear arms race. The first support the World Health Organization's renewed mandate to study the health effects of nuclear weapons and war led by the Republic of the Marshall Islands, Samoa and Vanuatu. The 2025 World Health Assembly overwhelmingly adopted a resolution to restore this mandate for the first time in three decades. With advances in radiation science and epidemiology since the WHO's last report over 30 years ago, this renewed study is a critical opportunity to document the full scope of harm and make recommendations on victim assistance and environmental remediation. We call on all WHO member states to support this work with both expertise and funding. Our second recommendation, ensure all recommendations and decisions made in this body and in every discussion of nuclear weapons legacy are made in consultation with affected communities. This should follow the Nuclear Truth Project's protocols centered on rights, respect, and reciprocity. Anything short of this risks further harm, further exploitation, and an incomplete and inaccurate record. Affected communities offer essential lived experience, expertise, and insight. We regret that more of our esteemed colleagues from affected communities do not have a seat at this table, and we thank those who joined us today. Our third recommendation, reevaluate and strengthen national, regional, and international victim assistance and environmental remediation programs, recognizing that all existing programs fall short of the scale of need and that nuclear armed states bear special responsibility. Assistance must be sustained, adequately funded, and responsive to the complex and evolving needs of survivors. This includes support for the Treaty on the Prohibition's ongoing work on victim assistance and environmental remediation through Articles 6 and 7. Distinguished delegates, as long as nuclear weapons still exist, so too does their threat. The abolition of nuclear weapons remains the only way to ensure that these disastrous impacts are not repeated, and we therefore call on all UN member states to join the Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons without delay. Let us be guided by past harms to prevent future ones. Thank you.

Kazakhstan and Kiribati for your leadership of this conference, especially as representatives of states whose people and communities have suffered greatly from nuclear testing. Reinvestment of resources toward victim assistance and environmental remediation is possible and necessary. Nuclear weapon nations are urged to respect the human right to life, to repair the harm, and commit to invest proportionally to their capacity, cognizant of their responsibility. Note that a total of $119 billion for nuclear weapons programs in preparation for use was spent by the nine nuclear weapon nation states in 2025, a 19% increase from the previous year. To advance victim assistance and environmental remediation as a moral duty and urgency for such a time as this is to true life so that we and all our descendants may live. Thank you.
I thank the representative of the United Religion Initiative for his statement. I now give the floor to Ms. Ri from the Solidarity for Peace and Reunification of Korea.

From recognition of accountability to nuclear justice, the voices of Korean atomic bomb victims, This is prepared by, the solidarity for peace and reunification of Korea, known as a spark. Korean atomic bomb victims were exposed to radiation within the historical context of Japan's occupation and colonial rule of the Korean Peninsula. Among all Korean victims, About 20% were laborers subject to forced mobilization under Japanese colonial rule. Upon returning home after liberation, surviving victims endured decades of suffering, afflicted by radiation-related illnesses, governmental neglect, social stigma, and severe poverty. The suffering caused by the atomic bombing continues to this day, 81 years later, yet the survivors call for their rights and realization of justice remain ignored. Furthermore, the trauma and after effects of the atomic bombings continue to affect the second and third generations. The voices of survivors must be meaningfully reflected in the international discussion on the victims assistance, including those under articles six and seven of the treaty on prohibition of nuclear weapons, TPNW. Currently, the primary demand of Korean atomic bomb survivors is the amendment of South Korea's Special Act on Support for Atomic Bomb Victims. Specifically, they are calling for, one, a comprehensive investigation into the actual conditions of victims and provisions of livelihood support. Two, official recognition of second and third generation victims who are currently excluded under the existing special act. And three, the establishment of memorial facilities and a peace park in Korea dedicated to atomic bomb victims. excluding Korean atomic bomb victims from international discussions on victims' assistance simply because South Korea is not yet a state party to the TPNW would add another hardship for them. This, at this tribunal, Korean survivors will testify to their past nuclear suffering while demanding recognition of responsibility and a formal apology, compensation and guarantees of non-repetition. Through this process, we aim to amplify the voices of Korean atomic bomb victims within the international community and contribute to achieving a denuclearized Korean peninsula and a world free of nuclear weapons. Thank you.
I thank the representative of SPARC for her statement. I now give the floor to Ms. Marie Hinault from the Manhattan Project for a Nuclear-Free World.

Thank you very much, co-chairs. This is a joint statement from Hiroshima Alliance for Nuclear Weapons Abolition, HANWA, and Mahan Project for Nuclear Free World. HANWA's mission is to investigate the unprecedented inhumane suffering caused by the atomic bombings and all forms of nuclear harm resulting from the nuclear fuel cycle, to widely publicize the facts and to work toward their abolition. The mission of Mehan Project for Nuclear Free World is to undo the unconscionable labors of the original Mehan Project that unleashed nuclear weapons and nuclear energy upon the world. We have been collaborating with members of nuclear affected communities around the world to advance human rights centered policies that protect nuclear victims from the ongoing harms of nuclear colonialism. Last October, we co-organized the World Nuclear Victims Forum in Hiroshima. We extend our gratitude to promoting organizations as well as hundreds of individual and organizational donors whose contributions made the two-day conference possible. On the final day of the forum, we adopted the Hiroshima Declaration and Declaration of the Rights of World Nuclear Victims 2025, calling for a broader recognition of who is considered a nuclear victim and affirm fundamental rights that must be guaranteed. They also offer roadmaps and guidelines to prevent and mitigate ongoing and future nuclear harm with the goal of creating a world in which no more nuclear victims are created. In advancing victim assistance, we underscore key experiences, practical measures, priorities, and often overlooked principles in the declarations. Nuclear victims are not limited to those directly affected by the use and detonation of nuclear weapons. Nuclear harm also extends to communities impacted by nuclear weapons development, nuclear power plants, uranium-related activities, radioactive waste including depleted uranium weapons, and the broader nuclear fuel cycle and its associated forms of harm and oppression. We must recognize that all peoples have the right to not be exposed to ionizing radiation, that anyone can become a nuclear victim at any time unless we end the nuclear age, and that nuclear and humanity cannot coexist. We need to condemn the long history of nuclear perpetrators who have downplayed or continue to downplay the risks of radiation exposure to protect the interests of the nuclear industry. It is essential that these perpetrators acknowledge responsibility, issue apologies to nuclear victims, provide compensation for past damage, establish necessary safety net for the nuclear victims and affected communities, and guarantee that no further nuclear harm is inflicted in the future. Affected people-centered approaches must take priority over the interest of responsible industries. Access to accurate information regarding the dangers of ionizing radiation exposure is also crucial. For example, no level of radiation exposure is without health risk. With regard to policies on environmental remediation, the rights of nuclear workers and those working in radioactively contaminated environments must also be protected. The Declaration on the Rights of World Nuclear Victims 2025 is available in English, French, German, and Japanese and can be downloaded from our website. Thank you very much.
I thank the speaker for the joint statement. I now give the floor to Dr. Zia Mian from Princeton University.

Thank you. I'm grateful for the opportunity to present a set of recommendations to this meeting on behalf of Professor Moritz Koot from the University of Hamburg, Professor Sebastian Philipp from the University of Wisconsin-Madison, and myself from the Program on Science and Global Security at Princeton University. All three of us are members of the Scientific Advisory Group of the Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons. This set of recommendations to this meeting draws on the work by this scientific advisory group. And the group has discussed issues of victim assistance and environmental remediation since it was established in 2023 and has made specific detailed recommendations on these matters in its reports in 2023 and 2025 to the respective meetings of states parties to the treaty and are available on the UNODA websites for those meetings. The following specific recommendations to this meeting are premised on the recognition that from a scientific point of view, there are shortcomings in the current understanding of the humanitarian and ecological consequences of nuclear weapon activities, including production, testing, and use, and in efforts to address fully those consequences. Also, that there is a disproportionate impact on nuclear weapon activities and the resulting environmental contamination, especially explosions, on indigenous people, non-self-governing people, women and girls. And finally, that we are not speaking in place of impacted communities and persons. These recommendations are limited to advancing victim assistance and environmental remediation. to address the impacts of the use and testing of nuclear weapons and other nuclear explosive devices. Similar efforts are needed to address past and ongoing harms caused by other nuclear weapon activities. Our first recommendation is the need for a global public archive of legacy radiological fallout monitoring data. United Nations member states and international organizations possess legacy data from nuclear fallout monitoring programs during and after the period of atmospheric nuclear testing. They also possess radiological monitoring data relevant for the delayed effects of testing and from nuclear weapons production. So in 2023, our group proposed collecting, curating, and sharing this data in a global public archive. This would be highly valuable to scientists and impacted communities to reconstruct past contamination of communities, environments, and ecologies, focus current assessments for assistance and remediation, and identify areas of future concern where land use changes and climate change may raise renewed contamination concerns. This legacy nuclear fallout data archive could be managed by the United Nations bodies such as the UN Scientific Committee on the Effects of Atomic Radiation or the Comprehensive Nuclear Test Ban Treaty Organization. Our second recommendation is we need a global database of the radionuclides actually associated with nuclear weapon test explosions. A full accounting of environmental contamination needs a database that includes information on nuclear weapon tests including dates, locations, altitudes, depths, yields, explosion types, the fissile material that was used, the radionuclide inventory, as well as what was known about atmospheric releases and known contamination. This will require additional declassification of relevant data by nuclear testing states. Our third recommendation is the need for regular reviews of radiological contamination of areas impacted by nuclear weapon testing. The UN Scientific Committee on the Effects of Atomic Radiation and the International Atomic Energy Agency have studied radiological contamination in areas impacted by nuclear weapon testing, either through literature studies or on site visits. Many of these investigations date back decades. And in the meantime, relevant scientific understanding and tools have advanced significantly. It would benefit impacted communities to have comprehensive field-based studies of the current contamination status of all past nuclear test sites with regular five-year reviews to track changes in contamination conditions. Our fourth recommendation is the need for planning for victim assistance and environmental remediation. Since 2006, the UNDP, together with partners, has engaged in hundreds of victim assistance and environmental remediation initiatives in regions of Belarus contaminated by radionuclides released in the 1986 Chernobyl nuclear power plant disaster. significant relevant experience in dealing with some of the issues of victim assistance and environmental remediation from nuclear weapon testing, UNDP could be mandated to study and develop plans for projects for communities in areas impacted by weapon testing. To complement this, we propose a resource guide of UN and international and national organisations and non governmental agencies with regard to victim assistance and environmental remediation. We need a catalogue of who can help. And we propose that it would be useful to compile a comprehensive list of UN and other bodies with capabilities to assist victims and remediate the environment. Our final recommendation is the need for official UN status and a mechanism for impacted communities to foster inclusion of these impacted communities and strengthen their voice within the UN framework. One option would be the UN Department of Economic and Social Affairs, Division for Inclusive Social Development. This division already supports inclusion of persons with disabilities, persons marginalized from society and development, and indigenous people. And we also recommend that the Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights appoint a special rapporteur on the protection and rights of communities impacted by nuclear weapon production, testing, and use, similar to that for indigenous people. Thank you for your attention.
I thank the speaker for their statement. Now I give the floor to Professor Matthew Pouton from Pace University.

Thank you, Chair. Faculty associated with Pace University's International Disarmament Institute have conducted relevant research to this meeting visiting communities impacted by nuclear weapons in Japan, Kiribati, Marshall Islands, Mohi Nui, or French Polynesia,

Fiji,

Cook Islands and Aboriginal Australia, and contributing also to global surveys like the Norwegian People's Aid report Is it Safe? Our research finds that nuclear violence is entwined with other forms of political repression, including the ongoing legacies of colonialism. Useful precedents exist in similar platforms in the biodiversity and Paris climate agreement. Policy making, financing and implementation require affected communities' free, prior, informed and ongoing consent. The UN Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples, as well as the CRPD, CEDAW and CRC provide guidance for ensuring human rights remain priorities. Human rights-centered assistance to victims is not just about compensation, medical care and rehabilitation, but also psychosocial support, socioeconomic inclusion and transitional justice processes. Our own work, at Pace University has improved through engagement with the Nuclear Truth Project protocols, which I think are available on the table down there, which guide outsiders' interactions with affected communities. We have found that affected communities have deep and underappreciated expertise arising from their experience of nuclear violence. We invite other scientists, researchers, diplomats, and advocates to engage with the Nuclear Truth Project protocols, building relationships of rights, respect, and reciprocity with nuclear-affected communities. Credible funding and technical assistance are crucial, but positive impact in affected communities depend on effective implementation. Donor-initiated projects that replicate existing initiatives can waste precious resources. And so states not yet party to the TPNW can engage with its positive obligations, including its proposed international trust fund, in a spirit of bridge-building. Civil society and academia serve as independent sources of information. However, independent analysis is limited by nuclear weapons programs' obfuscation. To build credibility, nuclear-armed states can declassify and make accessible relevant documents. Non-nuclear armed states that monitored fallout or contamination can also make their archives available. Finally, many affected communities express a desire for apology and restitution for harm, as well as a commitment to non-repetition. Such practices are relevant for any state, or institution, including the UN, complicit in one way or another with nuclear violence. Strong prohibitions, such as those in the TPNW, institutionalize guarantees not to use or test nuclear weapons again. A full version of these remarks will be available online. Thank you.

This is a story of my family, and perhaps my own story began long before I was born. My great-grandmother was born in 1932 in the village of Karaul near the Semipalatinsk nuclear test site. When construction of the test site began, her family was relocated to the village of Charma, about 380 kilometers away. On August 29, 1949, when the first nuclear test took place, she was pregnant. Her first long-awaited child, a baby girl, was stillborn. Her second child did not live to see his first birthday. Her third and fourth children also died very young. Imagine what that must have been like for my great-grandmother, each time preparing a cradle, sewing tiny shirts, waiting for a child, and each time having to take a grave for her own child, four times. When my great-grandmother was born, the fifth child, the family was already afraid that she would not survive later. She survived, but the health problems remained. Several of my great-grandmother's children had severe hearing loss, and three of them became disabled because of it. Seeing how sick her children were, my great-grandmother went to work as a construction worker to help build the first hospital in the district, hoping that at least there someone might receive treatment and survive. Later, my mother was born in that very hospital. Today, my mother is 44 years old. She has lived with severe hearing loss since childhood. In one ear, she has only about 10% hearing, and in another, about 50%. She also lives with type 1 diabetes and is insulin dependent. My great mother later developed cancer and is no longer alive. And then I was born. I became a continuum of this story. I spent almost my entire childhood in hospitals and rehabilitation centers. There were children there with even more severe diagnosis. They became my friends. And that was when I first began asking myself, what can I do for children like them? That's how I started helping other children. I created projects for children with disabilities and began developing an artificial intelligence application for children with speech disorders so that other people could understand them, because I know what it feels like to speak and still not be understood. At the same time, I began learning more about the sympathetic nervous system and the history of my own family. And the more I learned, the more I realized how many questions still remain unanswered. I consider myself part of the fourth generation of a family living with this nuclear legacy. But there is no official recognition of the fourth and subsequent generations as affected pollutions. And the next generation is already being born. We still do not know enough about what happens to the health of families decades after nuclear testing. What is truly connected to the consequences of radiation exposure? Which risks can be identified earlier? Which consequences can be prevented? These questions cannot be answered by assumptions. They must be answered by science. But for that, we need data, long-term research, and systematic health monitoring. Because the absence of an answer does not mean the absence of a problem. Behind every one of these questions is not a statistic. There is a person. There is a family. There is a mother who one day walks into a doctor's office and asks, Why did this happen to my child, just as my mother once did? And today, I want to propose counter steps. We can begin with something very simple, and one question to medical protocols. Did you or your ancestors live near a nuclear testing site? And in Kazakhstan, this could be made more specific. Did you or your ancestors live near a simulated nuclear test site? Just one question. But it could become the first step towards systematic screening and national database and a deeper understanding of the health of families connected to nuclear affected regions. Then we need more systematic measures. First, long-term. health monitoring of subsequent generations. Second, serious scientific research and discussion of the official recognition of new generation of affected people, because the absence of recognition does not mean that these people do not exist. Third, real assistance, access to medical examination, treatment, rehabilitation, support from families, and fair compensation mechanisms. At the same time, assistance should not depend only on whether a person lives today. Today, some forms of support, including additional environmental leave and certain employment benefits, are tied to residents in a specific affected territory. But a person may move from Chernobyl to another city. There are other changes, but their health history does not disappear. Their family history does not disappear. So in my view, this system should consider not only where a person lives today, but also their connection to an affected region. And fourth, we need to continue restoring the land because the site is not only a place of tragedy, it is our land, and it is incredibly beautiful. We need to research radiation monitoring and technologies that can help safely restore contaminated areas. But I also see another opportunity, educational tourism. Today, the Semipalatinsk test site can already be visited through organized routes. I want this area to develop further. I want people to come not for sensation, but for knowledge, so that school children, students, researchers, and people from different countries can see this history with their own eyes, hear the stories of affected families, understand the real human cost of nuclear weapons, so that this land becomes not only a place of remembrance, but also a place of education, research, and learning for future generations. And yes, I still have one very simple dream, that one day people will be able to come there with a thermos of tea and picnic blanket, sit on said land, and not be offended, because this land deserves more than memory, it deserves a future. But assistance to affected people is not only about medicine, compensation or benefits. It is also about dignity. Because of her health problems, my mother has faced losing her job, and that is why it is especially important to me that people from affected communities are not seen only as victims. We are not only people who need help, we can be researchers, entrepreneurs, teachers, professionals, we can create solutions. We have knowledge and lived experiences that cannot be found only in scientific articles or statistics. That's why affected communities should not only be objects of research. We should participate in research. We should not only tell our stories and international events. We should also participate in designing assistance programs and making decisions because our lived experiences is also expertise. When people are asking what is the meaning of your life, many others answer without hesitation, my children. Then take a moment and think. What will we pass on to them? What kind of land, what kind of knowledge, what kind of future, and what change will each of us be able to call our own? People can speak, but they do not always enter into dialogue. They can hear. but they do not always listen. They can see, but sometimes they fail to notice what is right in front of them. Once I could not speak. Today I have a voice. And today I use it not only to tell the story of my family. I speak for myself, for those who are no longer here, for those living with this legacy today, and for those who have not yet been born, because our legacy is not only what was left to us, our legacy is what we choose to leave behind. Thank you.

Yep, thank you, good chair, for, yeah, it's working. for inviting to be part of this panel and especially thanks Diana for such heartbreaking story and setting the scene for the future discussion. While today's meeting focusing on victim assistance and environmental remediation, the contribution is guided by its constitutional mandate in public health. does not implement victim assistance programs or environmental activities. I would like to just give a brief overview of WHO's work in the field of nuclear and radiation emergencies, which is focused on the public health response in line with our mandate. Radiation emergencies are rare. However, the consequences may affect the well-being of thousands of people and have very serious environmental and social economic impacts. We remember the nuclear accidents at Chernobyl in 1986 and Fukushima in 2011, where thousands were relocated, lost homes and livelihoods, and experienced impacts on their health and well-being. Radiation emergency scenarios can range from an isolated incident involving misplaced radioactive sources to a mass casualty event involving a nuclear detonation, whether a nuclear weapon or an improvised nuclear device. While international systems and standards for preparedness and response to nuclear emergencies at nuclear installations are well established, it is much more challenging to be fully prepared for unexpected acts. This is why investment in preparedness, strengthening capacities to prevent, monitor, detect, and response remain our critical importance, particular for the health sector, as health workers will be the frontline providers for clinical management and public health response. The international health regulations apply to all types and sources of health emergencies, including radiation emergencies. In line with its mandate to protect human health, WHO works with member states to strengthen national capacities for radiation emergency response. This includes medical response such as diagnosis and clinical management of radiation injuries, public health measures including iodine to roin blocking, sheltering, evacuation, food and drinking water safety, hospital preparedness and risk communication, as well as long-term health follow-up and mental health and psychological support. To fulfill its role in this area, the WHO established RAMPAN, the Radiation Emergency Medical Preparedness and Assessment Network. RAMPAN brings together leading specialists and institutions to support member states in preparedness, response and recovery following radiation emergency. Its expert contributes to the WHO guidance, norm standards, and other tools to support training for health workers. Given the multi-sectoral nature of radiation emergency response, the WHO also works with international organization, NGOs, professional societies, and other partners to ensure coordination at all levels. WHO also had a long history of examining the health consequences of nuclear weapons. In 2013, WHO also contributed to the study and report, The Illusion of Safety, which explored the preparedness for a nuclear detonation scenario and raised an important question, are we really prepared? The resolution called for an updated evidence-based building on WHO reports and incorporating more recent scientific knowledge, including long-term health impact, mental health, effects on health system and supply chains, and one-day consequences for populations. WHO is requested to report on progress in implementing this resolution to the World Health Assembly in 2029. This work will provide a modern and comprehensive reassessment of the consequences of nuclear war for public health and strengthen the evidence base available for member states and international community. Thank you, Madam Co-Chair. The ICRC is grateful to participate in this discussion on victim assistance and environmental remediation, experiences, lessons learned, and international cooperation. 81 years ago, the ICRC received the following cable from our delegate in Japan just after his arrival in Hiroshima on the 29th of August, 1945. Conditions appalling. City wiped out. 80% of all hospitals destroyed or seriously damaged. Inspected two emergency hospitals, conditions beyond description. Effects of bomb mysteriously serious. Many victims apparently recovering suddenly suffer fatal relapse due to decomposition of white blood cells and other internal injuries, now dying in great numbers. Estimated over 100,000 wounded in emergency hospitals located in surroundings sadly lacking bandaging materials, medicines. The eventual toll was not 100,000 wounded, but 140,000 dead by the end of 1945, increasing further to 320,000 since, and hundreds of thousands more hibakusha living with the physical and mental scars of the tragedy they had survived. Nagasaki was no different. Since 1945, the destructive power of nuclear weapons has increased many thousands of times. However, The capacity of states and emergency responders to provide assistance to the victims has not. The catastrophic humanitarian impacts of nuclear weapons are simply beyond the capacity of any humanitarian organization to address effectively. In 2024, the ICRC, the Belgian and Norwegian Red Cross societies, and Norwegian People's Aid hosted two conferences in Brussels and Oslo highlighting the humanitarian consequences if nuclear weapons were to be used today, as mentioned by Norway during the general exchange of views today. These conferences brought together hundreds of top experts and policymakers for an evidence-based analysis of the risks of nuclear weapon use. the short and long-term humanitarian impacts and available capacities to respond to the hypothetical use of just one 100-kiloton nuclear detonation over a capital city. They confirmed that the horrific scenes we witnessed in Hiroshima 81 years ago would be the same. Tens of thousands of people would die immediately, while hundreds of thousands would suffer horrific burn and blast injuries and radiation poisoning. Little or no help would be available to the population in or near the city centers who would have to fend for themselves or find their way to areas dozens of kilometers away from the detonation epicenter. Even there, services would still be overwhelmed by limited resources, likely loss of communications, and radiation risks. There would only be a handful of specialized burn beds in hospitals for the treatment of many thousands of severely burned victims. Many of the decision-makers needed to mount a coherent response from government, emergency response, and military circles would be among the dead. This gruesome reality must be at the center of nuclear debates and decision-making. The ICRC considers that it is extremely doubtful that nuclear weapons could ever be used in accordance with the principles and rules of international humanitarian law. In particular, we have serious doubts that any use of nuclear weapons could comply with the rules on distinction between civilians and military objectives, the principle of proportionality, the prohibition of superfluous injury and unnecessary suffering, and the rules protecting the natural environment in armed conflict. For years, we have called on all states to ensure that for humanitarian reasons, nuclear weapons are never used again, regardless of their views on the legality of use. The ICRC can also bring to this discussion its wider experience and lessons learned in assisting people affected by armed conflict in general. We know that victims of armed conflict require a comprehensive system of first aid, emergency care, primary health care and hospital services, as well as physical rehabilitation and mental health and psychosocial support. The ICRC aims to ensure that our humanitarian work builds up people's resilience in situations of vulnerability and crisis. When it comes to international cooperation, protecting humanity requires courage, commitment, and concerted action. The best way to put humanity first is by prohibiting and eliminating nuclear weapons. The most developed framework of international cooperation on victim assistance is developed in Article 7 of the Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons. Article 7.5 foresees various channels through which international assistance can be offered. As such, it can serve as a useful guide for states parties to understand how they can benefit from the expertise of other institutions or organizations, including the ICRC and the broader International Red Cross and Red Crescent Movement. For example, the Japanese Red Cross Society has been running hospitals for nuclear bomb survivors in Hiroshima since 1956, and in Nagasaki since 1969, where it still treats patients suffering from the long-term effects of exposure to ionizing radiation. The ICRC published a briefing note on the obligation to assist victims and remediate the environment within a shared responsibility under the TPNW. We encourage all states, whether or not they are a party to the TPNW, to consider this note as a useful tool for interpretive guidance on victim assistance and environmental remediation. The ICRC laments that tremendous financial and humanitarian resources continue to be invested in modernizing and maintaining nuclear weapons, resources that could instead be dedicated to supporting victims and remediating past harms to the environment. We urge those relying on nuclear weapons as part of their national security strategies to recognize that nuclear weapons are seen as a source of insecurity for most of the world. Increased efforts are needed to raise awareness among the public and policymakers about the catastrophic humanitarian consequences of nuclear weapons and the persistent risk that, as long as they exist, they might be used. While a vast amount of knowledge is already available, further evidence-based research is needed to better understand several elements, including the disproportionate impact on women and children, possible effects on second and further generation children of those exposed, and the cascading effects that nuclear weapon use would have on the natural environment and society at large. In closing, many individuals and communities continue to suffer daily as a result of past nuclear activities. The ICRC calls on all states to continue their collective efforts to ensure that affected individuals and communities can experience sustainable care and support today and tomorrow. Thank you.

So, can you hear? I would like to thank Kazakhstan and Karabass for their leadership on today's important topics. And I would like to thank the UNODA for the kind invitation to participate in this panel. I'm representing a small educational and research center at Columbia University called the K=1 Project, dedicated primarily to training undergraduate students on nuclear issues. After the end of the Cold War, there was a rise in ignorance on the topic of nuclear weapons, especially among the younger generation. And the K equal one project was created to address this concern. I'm a professor of physics at Columbia University right here in New York City. And I've spent most of my career studying particle physics and trying to understand what happened right after the big bang. At a glance this has no relevance to today's topic. But as so often happens studying fundamental science spins off in unanticipated directions. Nuclear weapons themselves are just such a spinoff. The laboratories where I've worked throughout my career, Conseil Europeen pour la Recherche Nuclaire, or CERN, in Geneva, Switzerland, and the Stanford Linear Accelerator Center at SLAC in Silicon Valley here in the US, have the world's highest energy particle accelerators, which have the potential to irradiate and contaminate local environments and communities. Both laboratories have enormous radiation safety teams dedicated to ensuring that such radiation exposure does not happen. With the Columbia K equals one project, we actually tapped into this expertise and transferred the detectors and the technologies developed at these major laboratories to make radiation measurements in the Marshall Islands, a country severely contaminated by nuclear weapons as we've heard this morning and from the young representative of the Marshallese community. I first visited the Marshall Islands in 2014 and have traveled there more than a dozen times, including on several research expeditions to the Northern Marshall Islands, where the US detonated 67 nuclear weapons, including 24 hydrogen bombs. It's important to point out that the US Department of Energy, which is in charge of developing and maintaining the US nuclear arsenal, and in particular the department's Livermore Lab, have already spent decades with similar advanced technologies making radiation measurements in the Marshall Islands and publishing their results. Therefore, our work funded entirely by Columbia University represented an effort independent of any government to ascertain the current radiological conditions. What we found was a complex picture. We conducted various measurements on four different Marshallese atolls, two of which had been used as testing sites and two of which were contaminated from radiation fallout, in particular from the infamous Bravo test. We saw no elevated radiation on one of the atolls called Utirik, and a mixed picture on one atoll called Eniwetok, which you've heard about earlier today, and high levels of radiation on two atolls called Bikini and Rongelap. A second crucial point I would like to make regards communication. I was invited by the Marshall Islands President Hilda Heine in 2017 in her first term to give a talk at a conference that her government organized on their March 1 Bravo Remembrance Day with several hundred Marshallese attendees in the capital Majuro right before launching our largest study. At the talk, I showed a photograph of my six-year-old son on a beach. And I said that I would travel to numerous islands on four atolls in the north of the country and make radiation measurements. I further promised that at the end of the project, I would let them know in each case whether I would let my son live on a particular island. No fancy scientific numbers, just a definitive statement on safety based upon the love of my own child. The promise was published on the front page of that week's Marshall Islands Journal. It turns out to be extremely difficult to certify that a potentially contaminated island is safe for children. On the other hand, it's very easy to identify that an island is clearly contaminated, should not be home to a multi-generational community. Let's just say that I would not let my son live on Bikini Island. Looking towards the future and in the context of the goals of this meeting, I have three recommendations or suggestions. First, the UN should investigate and consider recommending universal radiation safety standards, in particular for food safety. There is little consensus among different states on this topic today. Second, and related to the first, One cannot trust computer simulations that are not validated by experimental measurements. That means explicitly that one must make experimental measurements in situ on the island, in the food, soil, ocean sediment, and the surrounding environment to evaluate safety. Excellencies, delegates, colleagues, friends, translators, I speak today not only as an academic and a board member of the Nuclear Truth Project, but also as a French woman, a citizen of the country that has detonated 17 nuclear weapons in Algeria and 193 nuclear and thermonuclear weapons in Moruroa, French-occupied Polynesia. This January, we commemorated 30 years since the last French nuclear detonation. But the contamination from these French bombs has not ended. We are gathered today to discuss affected communities' needs for assistance. But communities affected by French fallout have never agreed to be nuked. France started its nuclear tests in Algeria in the midst of the Algerian war for independence, without consulting the Algerian people, nor listening to the opposition from downwind African countries. When the tests were moved to French-occupied Polynesia, A decision was not submitted to a local vote either, and neither the population nor its elected assembly members were consulted. This exclusion of indigenous people from democratic processes continues to this day. Even at the United Nations, there are no Moheli and Amazigh representatives representing their frontline communities in this room. This can be avoided as outlined by the Nuclear Truth project protocols, which you can find on the table down here. Given the colonial and racist history of French nuclear testing, we cannot in good faith use the word victims' assistance. We should speak of affected communities, and we have spoken today of affected communities' quest for justice. In the justice system, they're not only victims, they're also criminals. Countries in the Sahara and the Pacific are still very far from obtaining justice. France has never acknowledged its nuclear crimes, let alone apologized for them. The official doctrine for more than 50 years was that France had developed the world's one and only clean bomb, whose fallout did not fall. Relentless activism by affected communities forced Paris to recognize in the last decade a small number of dirty tests. Yet when President Macron visited Tahiti in 2021, he told Polynesians that the military had been unaware of the risks. Unaware in the 1960s, when three other nuclear powers had agreed to stop testing in the atmosphere altogether. France knew that its bomb would kill, but it lied and it continues to lie. On reparations, we fall short again. The actual compensations law, called the Morin Law, was put in place very belatedly in 2010, half a century after the French nuclear explosions began. More than 95% of claims were rejected in the first decade. The process remains opaque and scientifically contested, and it still leaves most claimants without access to compensation. As outlined by previous speakers, the list of recognized radiation diseases is woefully short, 23 cancers and nothing else. It does not address the disproportionate suffering borne by women who face recurring sterility, miscarriages, who give birth to babies unable to survive, who care for children and family members with chronic disease. It compensates neither the trauma of living in a contaminated environment, nor the fear of transmitting disease to one's offspring. Algeria and Mohenoui now stand at a decisive moment. A proposal adopted unanimously by the French National Assembly in January could replace the fraught 2010 compensation law. It carries real hard-won gains pushed by frontline communities. Victims would automatically obtain compensation for select radiation-induced diseases instead of having to prove their exposure to arbitrarily defined levels of radiation. But this proposed law also narrows who counts as a victim. Only Polynesian claimants born before the beginning of underground tests in 1975 would be eligible, when the current admittedly fraught law, at least admits those born until 1998. This is a 23-year contraction that writes off an entire generation. This new cutoff date survives neither scientific nor ethical scrutiny. The French military itself has acknowledged that several underground detonations leaked into the Pacific Ocean and entered the food chain. Radioactivity did not stop in 1975, nor in 1998 for that matter, and plutonium's half-life of 24,100 years will outlast every deadline a legislature can write. The double standard is starker still beside Algeria. There, the same law compensates victims of the underground tests. In Polynesia, where the underground tests were more numerous and more powerful, there would be no compensation? Why? This matters here as world leaders gather to discuss the consequences of nuclear proliferation. The proposed 1975 cutoff for compensation comforts France in its attempt to relegate nuclear testing to a bygone chapter of its history. France wants to dissociate the atrocity of its nuclear tests from its current nuclear proliferation. France wants us to dissociate the painful deaths under nuclear detonations from its glossy plans to modernize its nuclear arsenal. But affected communities, concerned academics, and informed citizens refuse that division. We refuse to separate the nuclear war that has already happened from the nuclear apocalypse that threatens us all. To conclude, France has been reticent to follow global calls for nuclear disarmament, threatening the whole world with its nuclear arsenal. But we cannot afford to wait any longer. So I come to you with a request to establish an international trust fund for the victims of nuclear testing and ensure that colonized territories like Mohi Nui can access it even when a colonial power such as France is reticent to ratify the TPNW. irradiated people are dying. We need justice now. Thank you.

On behalf of the co-chairs, I would also like to thank the interpreters, conference officers and all secretariat colleagues who supported the organization of this meeting. Finally, I would like once again to thank my distinguished co-chair Ambassador Humero, as well as our civil society coordinator, the Nuclear Age Peace Foundation, for their close cooperation in preparing for and supporting today's meeting. And this brings us to the end of our work. As mandated by the General Assembly in resolution 79/60, which hints at the encourages participants to produce a series of recommendations based on discussions, the co-chairs would like to note the encouraging nature of this provision. At the same time, Given the limited time and resources available, it has not been possible to undertake a consultation process with a view to developing a formally agreed outcome document. The co-chairs will therefore prepare a summary of their observations on the recommendations raised by participants during the meeting, without prejudice to any national positions. The summary will be submitted to the secretariat consistent with resolution 79/60. The meeting is adjourned. Thank you.
